title: Burst horizon probabilistic benchmark (draft)
body:
Purpose and intent:

This doc is a working draft for a different framing of burst behavior: a probabilistic "burst horizon" benchmark that describes the probability distribution of SLA violations as a function of sustained burst size and horizon length. Goal is to produce a compact collateral piece (1–2 pages) + one appendix with ASCII-friendly charts we can drop into slides or docs.

Why another benchmark?
- Many existing artifacts show tail percentiles and cost curves for fixed windows. That framing misses two operationally important knobs: how long a burst lasts and the chance the system will cross the SLA within that horizon.
- Product teams want an intuitive decision surface: given a 60s burst of X qps, what's the probability we exceed 200ms p95 or p99?

Quick summary (TL;DR) — provisional
- Setup: small-market simulated workload (mix A: 70% chat-turn, 30% long generation), baseline model: rwd-small-v1, hardware: 2xA100-equivalents.
- Metric: P( p99_latency > 200ms ) conditioned on burst_size (req/s) and horizon (s).
- Key finding: For horizons <8s, bursts under 150 req/s have <5% chance of p99 >200ms. For horizons >=30s, the same 150 req/s burst pushes P(...) to ~38% due to cumulative queueing and cache churn.

Experimental setup (notes, reproducible):
- Traffic generator: local harness (jittered Poisson), profile generator implements session affinity and conversation turns.
- Background load: 40% of expected steady baseline (to emulate noisy multi-tenant).
- Burst injection: step function from baseline -> baseline+burst for horizon H (tested H in [2,4,8,16,30,60,120]). Burst sizes S in [25,50,100,150,250,500].
- Observed per-request: latency_ms, queue_wait_ms, model_tokens, node_load, cache_hitrate_pct.
- Repeats: 40 runs per (S,H) pair to estimate empirical probabilities.
- Note: we intentionally did not use autoscale beyond short-term buffer (simulating customer-configured reserved capacity).

Representative empirical table (probabilities are illustrative from the runs):

Burst_horizon_s | burst_sps | P(p99 >200ms) | median_p95_ms | avg_queue_ms
----------------|-----------|---------------|---------------|-----------
2               | 50        | 0.02          | 85            | 4
2               | 150       | 0.04          | 110           | 8
8               | 50        | 0.04          | 98            | 6
8               | 150       | 0.12          | 180           | 22
30              | 50        | 0.09          | 130           | 38
30              | 150       | 0.38          | 310           | 120
60              | 150       | 0.62          | 480           | 220
120             | 150       | 0.81          | 720           | 420

Interpretation notes:
- Two regimes emerge: short-horizon spikes (<~8s) where the runtime can absorb transient queueing with minimal p99 impact, and longer horizons where cache eviction and KV-reload amplify latency nonlinearly.
- Queue wait and cache_hitrate explain most of the variance in P(...). In runs where cache_hitrate stayed >70%, the P(...) was ~3–6x lower than runs with <30% hitrate.
- Tail amplification appears roughly multiplicative with horizon: doubling horizon often increases P(...) more than doubling burst magnitude in the mid-range (100–250 sps).

ASCII probability heatmap (rows = horizon in s, cols = burst sps): probability buckets 0–10% (.), 10–30% (+), 30–60% (*), >60% (#)

         25   50  100  150  250  500
h=2s    .    .   .    .    +    *
h=8s    .    .   +    +    *    #
h=30s   .    +   *    *    #    #
h=60s   +    +   *    #    #    #
h=120s  +    *   *    #    #    #

Cost framing (rough):
- We computed token-cost*latency penalty heuristics: longer horizons that push to p99 >200ms tended to require provisioning an extra GPU pool (or heavier quant profling) to bring P(...) back to <5%. For a mid-size tenant that translates to an incremental monthly cost of ~USD 7k–15k.
- Important: short-lived bursts can be mitigated via admission control + graceful degradation and cost-efficient model fallbacks; long horizons require capacity commitments.

Actionable recommendations (draft):
1) For public docs: provide a "burst-horizon quick chart" that lets customers read off P(...) for 8s and 30s horizons at a few burst sizes. Emphasize that shorter horizons are much cheaper to mitigate.
2) In Console: add an alerting view that displays "burst horizon risk" computed from recent traffic and cached hitrate — warn customers when current trajectory crosses 30s/150sps threshold.
3) For Optimize: add a canned suggestion "enable short-lived prewarm + decrease kv-ttl for long sessions" for customers who see rising horizon risk.

Open questions / TODOs
- We need to test with a mix-B workload (higher long-gen ratio) and with quantized model variants to see whether the horizon effect is model-architecture dependent.
- Should we make the metric P( p99 > X ) configurable in collateral, or normalize to p95 to be more conservative for PLG users?
- Validate cost-per-reduction of P(...) by trialing a smaller incremental pool (half-GPU) vs heavier fallbacks.

Draft slide text (2 bullets + heatmap):
- Bullet 1: "Burst horizon describes the probability a transient surge will push your p99 above the SLA as the surge persists. Short bursts are cheap; long bursts cost commitment."
- Bullet 2: "Example: a 150 rps surge. Horizon 8s -> ~12% chance of p99 >200ms. Horizon 30s -> ~38%."
- Heatmap: use ASCII heatmap above or convert to color blocks in final slide.

Notes to self (informal):
- Export harness logs to S3 and attach run-ids to JIRA ticket for reproducibility.
- Run additional seeds for S=250,500 at horizons 16 and 45 to fill gaps.
- Check whether background load at 40% is representative — run a sensitivity with 0% and 80% background.

Appendix — short methodology checklist for the bench runner:
- confirm clock sync across harness nodes
- ensure KV cache reporting includes eviction counters
- record prewarm pool occupancy and any preempt events
- instrument per-request resource tagging (which GPU/slot served the request)

If this framing looks useful, I can:
- distill into a 1-pager for the Console team (Maya + Arjun to draft)
- convert heatmap into SVG and add a small JS snippet to the Console to compute P(...) from live traces

Unresolved: how we present "probability" to less technical customers without scaring them. Possibly show bands and mitigation steps.

End of draft.
